name: Axokine
lead: Axokine is a modified recombinant form of human ciliary neurotrophic factor (CNTF) that was developed as an obesity drug by Regeneron Pharmaceuticals. It carries a 15-amino-acid C-terminal truncation and two substitutions, and is reported to be more potent and stable than natural CNTF [7]. It was designed to reduce body weight through a leptin-like mechanism [4].

The weight-loss effect was discovered when CNTF given for motor neuron disease caused unexpected weight loss [7]. In phase III obesity trials around 2003, the average effect was small. According to Wikipedia, patients without antibodies lost about 12.5 pounds over a year versus 4.5 pounds on placebo, while nearly 70 percent developed antibodies to the drug after about three months [7]. It was not commercialised [7].
Axokine is not an appearance product or a looksmaxxing staple; it is included as a historical fat-loss compound. The sources contain no forum discussion of it.

paras: CNTF is a survival factor for neurons and acts through gp130/LIFR signalling and the Jak-STAT pathway in cells such as retinal neurons [2][5]. In db/db mice, the modified CNTF (Axokine) was reported to improve diabetic parameters and hepatic steatosis and to increase basal metabolic rate, in contrast with earlier work in which weight loss was mainly attributed to reduced food intake [4]. A separate study found CNTF prevented acute lipid-induced insulin resistance in peripheral tissues [8]. Axokine was listed among investigational anti-obesity agents in a 2004 review [3].

Human data in the sources come mainly from Wikipedia's account of the trials: phase III obesity trials run by Regeneron around 2003 showed a modest effect in patients who did not develop antibodies, and antibody formation in a large majority of participants was a major problem [7]. An earlier trial in ALS produced less improvement in muscle control than expected, along with appetite loss [7]. The sources reviewed do not report cosmetic or body-composition outcomes beyond weight.

CNTF and analogues were also studied for retinal degeneration. A 1998 mouse study tested several survival factors on degenerating photoreceptors [1], and repeated injections of a CNTF analogue were reported to give long-term photoreceptor survival in hereditary retinal degeneration in animals [9]. Wikipedia describes an implant, NT-501, secreting CNTF that reduced photoreceptor degradation in retinitis pigmentosa [7].

timeline.event: Unexpected weight loss noticed in a CNTF motor neuron disease study [7].

card.summary: A discontinued CNTF-based injectable for obesity that produced small weight loss in trials and triggered antibodies in most users.
card.note: Never commercialised; antibodies in about 70 percent of trial participants.

quick.overview:
Axokine is a modified version of CNTF, a nerve survival protein, that Regeneron developed for obesity after weight loss was noticed in an earlier trial.

In phase III trials the effect was modest, and most participants developed antibodies. It was not commercialised.
quick.mechanism: It was designed to lower body weight through a leptin-like mechanism, and in diabetic mice it was reported to raise metabolic rate beyond its effect on food intake.
quick.risks: Antibody formation against the drug was the major issue reported in trials. It is not an approved or marketed drug.
